kernels.definition: A mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and an ordered crystal structure; minerals are identified by physical properties such as hardness, streak, luster, and cleavage.

definitionAnchor.quote: naturally occurring, inorganic, solid at room temperature, regular crystal structure, and defined chemical composition

facts.text: Hardness is measured on the Mohs scale; diamond is a 10 and is about four times harder than corundum, a 9.

anchor.quote: Diamond defines a hardness of 10 and is actually about four times harder than corundum, which is 9

facts.text: Streak is the color of a mineral's powder, and is more reliable than the color of the whole specimen.

anchor.quote: Streak examines the color of a powdered mineral

facts.text: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding; minerals without such planes fracture irregularly.

anchor.quote: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along flat planes of weak bonding

facts.text: Luster describes how a mineral's surface reflects light — metallic, glassy, or dull.

anchor.quote: Luster describes how the mineral looks

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §3.1 What is a mineral; §3.5 Identifying minerals

kernels.definition: Silicate minerals, built from the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron, are the most abundant rock-forming minerals; the way tetrahedra link together defines the major silicate structures.

definitionAnchor.quote: Silicate minerals form the largest group of minerals on Earth, comprising the vast majority of the Earth's mantle and crust

facts.text: The silicon-oxygen tetrahedron (SiO4) is one silicon atom at the center bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners.

anchor.quote: The silicon-oxygen tetrahedron (SiO4) consists of a single silicon atom at the center and four oxygen atoms located at the four corners of the tetrahedron

facts.text: Tetrahedra link by sharing corner oxygen atoms into chains, sheets, or three-dimensional frameworks.

anchor.quote: Polymers are chains, sheets, or three-dimensional structures, and are formed by multiple tetrahedra covalently bonded via their corner oxygen atoms

facts.text: How much oxygen is shared between tetrahedra controls the silicate group — isolated tetrahedra, single chains, sheets, or frameworks like quartz.

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §3.1 Silicate minerals

kernels.definition: Igneous rock forms when molten magma or lava cools and crystallizes; how fast it cools controls crystal size, distinguishing coarse intrusive rocks from fine-grained extrusive rocks.

definitionAnchor.quote: Igneous rock is formed when liquid rock freezes into a solid rock

facts.text: Lava cooling quickly at the surface forms tiny crystals, while magma cooling slowly at depth forms large crystals.

anchor.quote: Lava cools quickly on the surface of the earth and forms tiny microscopic crystals

facts.text: Magma that cools slowly deep within the crust forms intrusive (plutonic) rock with a coarse-grained texture.

anchor.quote: If magma cools slowly, deep within the crust, the resulting rock is called intrusive or plutonic

facts.text: Lava cooling at or near the surface forms extrusive (volcanic) rock with a fine-grained texture.

anchor.quote: the resulting igneous rock is called extrusive or volcanic

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.1 Magma generation and igneous textures

kernels.definition: A volcano's eruptive style is set largely by magma viscosity, which rises with silica content: runny low-silica magma erupts gently, while sticky high-silica magma traps gas and erupts explosively.

definitionAnchor.quote: Silica content controls magma viscosity and the eruptive style of volcanoes

facts.text: Low-viscosity (low-silica, basaltic) magma flows easily like syrup, producing the gentle eruptions of Hawaiian shield volcanoes.

anchor.quote: Low viscosity magma flows easily more like syrup, the basaltic volcanism that occurs in Hawaii on shield volcanoes

facts.text: High-viscosity (high-silica, felsic) magma is thick and sticky and flows slowly like toothpaste, trapping gas until it erupts violently.

anchor.quote: High viscosity means a thick and sticky magma, typically felsic or intermediate, that flows slowly, similar to toothpaste

facts.text: The most dangerous volcanic hazard is the pyroclastic flow, a fast cloud of hot ash and gas typical of explosive high-silica volcanoes.

anchor.quote: The most dangerous volcanic hazard are pyroclastic flows

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4.4 Volcanic eruptions and hazards

kernels.definition: Weathering breaks bedrock into sediment in place, while erosion is the transport of that sediment away by water, wind, gravity, or ice.

definitionAnchor.quote: Weathering is a process that turns bedrock into smaller particles, called sediment

facts.text: Erosion is a mechanical process, driven by water, wind, gravity, or ice, that transports sediment.

anchor.quote: Erosion is a mechanical process, usually driven by water, wind, gravity, or ice, which transports sediment

facts.text: Mechanical weathering physically breaks bedrock into smaller pieces without changing its chemistry.

anchor.quote: Mechanical weathering physically breaks bedrock into smaller pieces

facts.text: Chemical weathering dissolves or alters minerals into new substances and dominates in warm, humid environments.

anchor.quote: Chemical weathering is the dominate weathering process in warm, humid environments

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §5.1 Weathering and erosion

kernels.definition: Sedimentary rock forms when sediment is deposited, compacted under burial, and cemented into stone — a process called lithification — and its features record the depositional environment.

definitionAnchor.quote: Deposition happens when friction and gravity overcome the forces driving sediment transport

facts.text: Compaction occurs as more material accumulates on top, squeezing the grains together.

anchor.quote: Compaction occurs when material continues to accumulate on top of the sediment layer

facts.text: Cementation glues the grains together with minerals; compaction and cementation together are lithification.

anchor.quote: Cementation is the process of cementing minerals coating the sediment grains and gluing them together

facts.text: Clastic (detrital) sedimentary rocks are made of pieces of preexisting weathered rock.

anchor.quote: Detrital or clastic sedimentary rocks consist of preexisting sediment pieces that comes from weathered bedrock

facts.text: The features of a sedimentary rock are read to reconstruct its original depositional environment.

anchor.quote: to understand the original depositional environment

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §5.3 Sedimentary rocks

mcItems.q: A hand sample is a naturally occurring, inorganic solid. It has a glassy surface, a definite composition, and breaks along flat planes. Which claim is warranted from these observations?
op: It is a mineral.
It is volcanic glass.
It is a sedimentary rock.
It is a weathered fragment.
mcItems.ex: The observations fit the mineral definition: naturally occurring, inorganic solid with definite chemical composition and an ordered crystal structure, and the flat breakage points to cleavage. The closest alternative is volcanic glass, but the packet supports a mineral identification from properties

mcItems.q: Two specimens look similar in hand sample, but the powder from one is red while the whole specimen is dark gray. Which observation is the best basis for identifying that specimen?
op: Its streak is red.
Its luster is metallic.
Its cleavage is perfect.
Its hardness is high.
mcItems.ex: Streak is the color of a mineral's powder and is more reliable than the color of the whole specimen. The most plausible misconception is to use the dark gray surface color, but the powder color is the supported identification clue here

keyTerms.df: Resistance to scratching measured on the Mohs scale, where larger numbers indicate harder minerals.
keyTerms.eg: Diamond ranks 10 on the Mohs scale and is about four times harder than corundum, which is 9.
keyTerms.mi: A mineral’s color alone tells its hardness.
keyTerms.cx: Color can vary, so hardness is identified with the Mohs scale instead.

keyTerms.df: Powder color produced when a mineral is rubbed on a streak plate; it is usually more reliable than surface color.
keyTerms.eg: A dark specimen that leaves a red powder has a red streak.
keyTerms.mi: Streak is just the same as the mineral’s outside color.
keyTerms.cx: The powder color is the diagnostic observation, not the hand-sample color.

mcItems.q: Two minerals contain the same SiO4 tetrahedra, but one forms chains and the other forms a framework. Which claim best explains the difference?
op: The amount of oxygen shared between tetrahedra controls whether they stay isolated or link into
Each tetrahedron has one silicon atom at the center bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners
Silicate minerals are the most abundant rock-forming minerals in Earth’s crust
Tetrahedra join only by sharing silicon atoms, so structure does not vary much
mcItems.ex: Correct: the degree of shared oxygen determines whether tetrahedra remain isolated or link into chains, sheets, or frameworks. The closest misconception is that the tetrahedra’s shape alone fixes the structure, but the source says the linkage pattern is controlled by how much oxygen is shared.

mcItems.q: A diagram shows one central silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms. Which claim is directly supported?
op: One silicon atom sits at the center and is bonded to four oxygen atoms at the corners
Four silicon atoms sit at the corners and bond to one oxygen atom in the middle
Shared oxygen atoms always make a three-dimensional framework
The mineral must be quartz because all silicates have the same linkage pattern
mcItems.ex: Correct: the observation matches the silicon-oxygen tetrahedron. The closest misconception is reversing the atom positions or jumping from one tetrahedron to a full framework, but the source packet only supports the single tetrahedron geometry here.

keyTerms.df: A basic silicate unit with one silicon atom centered among four oxygen atoms.
keyTerms.eg: A single SiO4 unit in a mineral structure diagram.
keyTerms.mi: It has four silicon atoms around one oxygen atom.
keyTerms.cx: The silicon is in the center; the oxygen atoms occupy the corners.

keyTerms.df: A three-dimensional network formed when tetrahedra share enough oxygen atoms to connect widely.
keyTerms.eg: Quartz has a framework structure.
keyTerms.mi: It means all silicate minerals are isolated tetrahedra.
keyTerms.cx: Frameworks are one linkage pattern, not the only one; silicates can also form chains or sheets.

mcItems.q: A sample has tiny crystals and was collected from a lava flow at the surface. Which claim is warranted?
op: It cooled quickly at the surface.
It cooled slowly deep underground.
It formed from sediment compaction.
It changed by weathering after burial.
mcItems.ex: Tiny crystals and a surface lava flow match rapid cooling at or near the surface, which produces extrusive rock with fine grains. The closest mistake is choosing slow cooling deep in the crust, but that would produce large crystals and coarse texture instead of tiny crystals.

mcItems.q: A hand sample from deep in the crust is coarse-grained. Which statement best fits the observation packet?
op: It is intrusive rock from slow cooling.
It is extrusive rock from fast cooling.
It is sedimentary rock from deposition.
It is metamorphic rock from pressure.
mcItems.ex: Coarse grains fit magma that cooled slowly at depth, forming intrusive plutonic rock. The most plausible misconception is to pick extrusive rock from fast cooling, but that would give fine-grained texture and tiny crystals at or near the surface.

keyTerms.df: Igneous rock that forms when magma cools slowly below the surface, producing a coarse-grained texture.
keyTerms.eg: A plutonic sample with large crystals found deep in the crust.
keyTerms.mi: Any rock with large crystals must be sedimentary.
keyTerms.cx: Large crystals can point to slow cooling of magma underground, not deposition.

keyTerms.df: Igneous rock that forms when lava cools quickly at or near the surface, producing a fine-grained texture.
keyTerms.eg: A volcanic lava flow that solidifies into a fine-grained basaltic rock.
keyTerms.mi: Fine grains always mean the rock formed under water.
keyTerms.cx: Fine grains can result from rapid cooling of lava at the surface, not from water deposition.

mcItems.q: A lava sample is low in silica and flows very easily. Which eruptive style is most warranted?
op: A gentle shield-volcano eruption
A thick, gas-trapping explosive eruption
A slow ash-and-gas surge
A lava dome collapse flow
mcItems.ex: Low-silica magma is low-viscosity and flows like syrup, which matches gentle Hawaiian shield eruptions. The closest alternative is the explosive eruption, but that requires sticky, high-silica magma that traps gas rather than running easily.

mcItems.q: An explosive volcano sends a fast cloud of hot ash and gas downslope. Which hazard is named?
op: A pyroclastic flow
A basaltic lava stream
A shield-volcano lava flow
A quiet volcanic gas release
mcItems.ex: A fast cloud of hot ash and gas is the pyroclastic flow hazard. The nearest distractor is the lava stream, but the observation describes a hot ash-and-gas cloud from an explosive high-silica volcano, not a slow-moving lava flow.

keyTerms.cx: Silica content changes viscosity: more silica usually makes magma stickier and less able to flow.

mcItems.q: A gravel bar downstream contains loose sand and pebbles that match nearby bedrock, but the rock itself is still exposed in place. Which claim is best warranted?
op: Weathering broke the bedrock into sediment at the source.
Erosion carried the sediment away from the source.
Chemical weathering created new minerals from the bedrock.
The sediment was deposited by melting ice.
mcItems.ex: The exposed bedrock plus loose sediment nearby supports breakage in place, which is weathering. The closest alternative is erosion, but that would require transport away from the source; the observation only shows sediment near the bedrock, not movement.

mcItems.q: After a year in a warm, humid region, a rock sample is found to have altered minerals rather than just smaller fragments. Which claim is best warranted?
op: Mechanical weathering shortened the rock into fragments.
Chemical weathering changed minerals into new substances.
Wind erosion transported the fragments downhill.

mcItems.q: Two minerals contain the same SiO4 tetrahedra, but one forms chains and the other forms a framework. Which claim best explains the difference?

mcItems.q: A sample has tiny crystals and was collected from a lava flow at the surface. Which claim is warranted?
op: It cooled quickly at the surface.
It cooled slowly deep underground.
It formed from sediment compaction.
It changed by weathering after burial.
mcItems.ex: Tiny crystals and a surface lava flow match rapid cooling at or near the surface, which produces extrusive rock with fine grains. The closest mistake is choosing slow cooling deep in the crust, but that would produce large crystals and coarse texture instead of tiny crystals.

mcItems.q: A hand sample from deep in the crust is coarse-grained. Which statement best fits the observation packet?
op: It is intrusive rock from slow cooling.
It is extrusive rock from fast cooling.
It is sedimentary rock from deposition.
It is metamorphic rock from pressure.
mcItems.ex: Coarse grains fit magma that cooled slowly at depth, forming intrusive plutonic rock. The most plausible misconception is to pick extrusive rock from fast cooling, but that would give fine-grained texture and tiny crystals at or near the surface.

keyTerms.df: Igneous rock that forms when magma cools slowly below the surface, producing a coarse-grained texture.
keyTerms.eg: A plutonic sample with large crystals found deep in the crust.
keyTerms.mi: Any rock with large crystals must be sedimentary.
keyTerms.cx: Large crystals can point to slow cooling of magma underground, not deposition.

keyTerms.df: Igneous rock that forms when lava cools quickly at or near the surface, producing a fine-grained texture.

keyTerms.mi: Fine grains always mean the rock formed under water.
keyTerms.cx: Fine grains can result from rapid cooling of lava at the surface, not from water deposition.

mcItems.q: A lava sample is low in silica and flows very easily. Which eruptive style is most warranted?
op: A gentle shield-volcano eruption
A thick, gas-trapping explosive eruption
A slow ash-and-gas surge
A lava dome collapse flow
mcItems.ex: Low-silica magma is low-viscosity and flows like syrup, which matches gentle Hawaiian shield eruptions. The closest alternative is the explosive eruption, but that requires sticky, high-silica magma that traps gas rather than running easily.

mcItems.q: An explosive volcano sends a fast cloud of hot ash and gas downslope. Which hazard is named?
op: A pyroclastic flow
A basaltic lava stream
A shield-volcano lava flow
A quiet volcanic gas release
mcItems.ex: A fast cloud of hot ash and gas is the pyroclastic flow hazard. The nearest distractor is the lava stream, but the observation describes a hot ash-and-gas cloud from an explosive high-silica volcano, not a slow-moving lava flow.

keyTerms.df: Resistance to flowing; in magma, higher values mean thicker, slower-moving material.
keyTerms.eg: Basaltic magma at a Hawaiian shield volcano is low-viscosity and runs easily.
keyTerms.mi: Any hot melted rock should move the same way.
keyTerms.cx: Silica content changes viscosity: more silica usually makes magma stickier and less able to flow.

keyTerms.df: A fast-moving mixture of hot ash and gas produced during explosive eruptions.
keyTerms.eg: A dense, scorching cloud racing down the flank of a high-silica volcano.
keyTerms.mi: It is just ordinary lava traveling downhill.
keyTerms.cx: Lava is molten rock that flows; a pyroclastic flow is an ash-and-gas hazard linked to explosive eruptions.
